metadata.file_name: 9. Alkan et al. (2025). Educational improvement through machine learning: Strategic models for better PISA scores.pdf
metadata.title: Educational improvement through machine learning: Strategic models for better PISA scores

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 data for 37 OECD countries and constructs domain-specific prediction targets based on standardized PISA scores in reading, mathematics, and science. The analytic dataset is further restricted by preprocessing steps: continuous student variables are categorized, variables deemed insignificant are removed, and countries are dichotomized into high- vs low-performing groups using OECD-average thresholds (487 reading, 489 mathematics, 489 science). The manuscript does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; instead, it applies Random Forest via R and performs feature selection using the Boruta package. Because Random Forest/Boruta are used without any stated survey-weight integration, the analysis should be interpreted as not fully accounting for PISA’s complex sampling design and clustering.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports using PISA 2018 standardized scores as outcomes and states that there was no missing data, but it does not describe any explicit missing-data handling procedure for the ML modeling pipeline (e.g., how any remaining missingness in predictors was treated, or whether cases were excluded after preprocessing). This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain some missingness in background variables and ML feature selection can be sensitive to how missing predictor values are handled. The authors’ statement of “no missing data” is not accompanied by a reproducible rule (which variables were checked, and at what stage).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The dataset consists of PISA 2018 scores for 37 OECD countries in science, reading, and mathematics, plus student-level background and attitudinal variables. Countries are categorized as high-performing vs low-performing using OECD-average thresholds (reading >487, mathematics >489, science >489), and a classification variable is created accordingly for each domain. The study then preprocesses predictors by converting continuous variables into categorical bins, coding/standardizing variable names, removing variables considered insignificant, and using only categorical variables (24 categorical variables listed in Table 2) for the Random Forest/Boruta pipeline. The manuscript states that there was no missing data at the time of analysis, but it does not provide a detailed exclusion rule beyond this statement.

main_findings.target_variable: Reading success classification (high vs low vs OECD average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest with Boruta feature selection; most important variables identified (no explicit accuracy/AUC reported). Highest mean importance coefficient: CPERWEEK (7.266618); highest coefficient estimate: CPERWEEK (0.844).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 reading data for 37 OECD countries, the study leveraged ICT access (ICTRES), foreign language lessons per week, total weekly teaching load, metacognition (credibility), and economic social cultural status to predict whether countries were above the OECD-average reading threshold. It found that ICT access and instructional time variables (especially CPERWEEK) were consistently among the most influential predictors, with CPERWEEK showing the highest importance and coefficient estimate. This indicates that strengthening students’ access to information technology and increasing/optimizing subject-specific instructional time may be associated with higher reading performance, though the Random Forest results are predictive and do not establish causal effects.

main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics success classification (high vs low vs OECD average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest with Boruta feature selection; most important variables identified (no explicit accuracy/AUC reported). Highest mean importance coefficient: COMPETE (7.060205); highest coefficient estimate: COMPETE (0.628).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 mathematics data for 37 OECD countries, the study leveraged academic competition (COMPETE), highest parental occupational status, metacognition (credibility), economic social cultural status, and ICT access (ICTRES) to predict whether countries were above the OECD-average mathematics threshold. It found that COMPETE and parental occupational status were among the strongest contributors, with COMPETE having the highest importance and coefficient estimate in the mathematics model. This indicates that policies that foster constructive competitive or performance-oriented learning environments in mathematics may align with higher mathematics outcomes, while causality cannot be inferred from the predictive model.

main_findings.target_variable: Science success classification (high vs low vs OECD average)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest with Boruta feature selection; most important variables identified (no explicit accuracy/AUC reported). Highest mean importance coefficient: METASPAM (8.875383); highest coefficient estimate: METASPAM (0.550).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 science data for 37 OECD countries, the study leveraged ICT access (ICTRES), total weekly teaching load, perceived PISA test difficulty, metacognition (credibility), and academic competition (COMPETE) to predict whether countries were above the OECD-average science threshold. It found that metacognition (METASPAM) was the strongest science-related predictor, while ICT access and instructional time also ranked highly across domains. This indicates that embedding metacognitive skill development and improving students’ learning conditions (including ICT access and adequate instructional time) may support science performance improvements, though the model remains non-causal and the paper does not report predictive validation metrics.

data.outcome_summary: This PLOS One study uses PISA 2018 data from 37 OECD countries and applies a Random Forest model with Boruta feature selection to identify influential predictors of country-level “success” (above vs below OECD-average thresholds) in reading, mathematics, and science. The authors report domain-specific top variables: ICT access (ICTRES) and instructional time (notably CPERWEEK) are prominent across domains, while metacognition (METASPAM) is especially important for science and academic competition (COMPETE) is especially important for mathematics. They provide coefficient estimates and mean importance coefficients for the selected variables, but they do not report standard predictive performance metrics such as accuracy, AUC, or RMSE for the classification models. Methodologically, the paper states there was no missing data and does not describe survey-weight or replicate-weight usage, which limits generalizability under PISA’s complex sampling design. Finally, the authors caution that Random Forest does not directly show causal relationships, so policy implications should be treated as associations rather than causal effects.
